status_summary: On 2025-05-14 in Abidjan the Senior Bureau Official of the Bureau of African Affairs launched a Commercial Diplomacy Strategy, framed as trade not aid, whose six actions include market reforms with governments in priority countries and commercially viable infrastructure projects; the remarks name no priority countries and describe the strategy's focus as countries where US companies want to do business and data support it. The National Security Strategy dated November 2025 and released in December 2025 calls for a transition in Africa from a foreign aid paradigm to an investment and growth paradigm and for partnering with select capable, reliable states, but names no focus countries. In December 2025 the State Department signed health compacts with eight African governments. The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (Pub. L. 119-75), signed 2026-02-03, extends AGOA duty-free treatment through 2026-12-31 in section 5019, retroactive to 2025-09-30 according to USTR.

timeline.event: The Senior Bureau Official of the Bureau of African Affairs launched a Commercial Diplomacy Strategy in Abidjan, framed as trade not aid, with six actions including market reforms with governments in priority countries and commercially viable infrastructure projects; the remarks name no priority countries.

timeline.event: The State Department signed bilateral health memorandums of understanding with eight sub-Saharan African governments (Cameroon, Eswatini, Kenya, Lesotho, Liberia, Mozambique, Rwanda and Uganda), beginning with Kenya, under the America First Global Health Strategy. (month-only date)
The White House released the National Security Strategy, which calls for a shift in Africa from aid to trade and investment and refers only generally to select partner states.

The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (Pub. L. 119-75) became law; its section 5019 extends AGOA duty-free treatment and the regional apparel and third-country fabric programs through 2026-12-31 (retroactive to 2025-09-30 per USTR).

title: Shift Africa policy from aid to private-sector growth with designated focus countries
uncertainties: The National Security Strategy's Africa section was read on whitehouse.gov: it favors capable, reliable states and select partners without listing them, and names countries only in conflict contexts (DRC and Rwanda, Sudan, Ethiopia, Eritrea and Somalia). Its cover is dated November 2025; the exact release date was not confirmed from the PDF. The AGOA extension was confirmed as section 5019 of Pub. L. 119-75 through Proclamation 11030 on the Federal Register host; the section text itself was not opened, and the proclamation does not address retroactivity, which rests on the USTR statement. The Commercial Diplomacy Strategy remarks were read in a 2026-10-19 check on the State Department Africa Regional Media Hub bulletin hosted by govdelivery, which dates them 2025-05-14 (bulletin sent 2025-05-15) and replaces a month-only date that rested on a news aggregator's story identifier; the remarks use the phrase priority countries without naming them or defining them beyond where US companies want to do business. The priority-country concept in the commercial strategy is the nearest match to the Mandate's focus countries, but it is limited to commercial engagement and no list was found. The eight health compacts are a global health selection, not a general focus-country designation, and their individual signing dates were not confirmed. In the same check, a State Department joint statement of 2026-01-28 with the African Union Commission on an investment working group and an annual program statement for a U.S.-Africa strategic investment program were seen only on a news aggregator page and an anonymous file-storage copy, not on state.gov or grants.gov, so they are not relied on; the America First Global Health Strategy (September 2025) could not be read because the archived copy on web.archive.org was blocked, and its figures, reported by an external retrieval, are not used. The aid-to-growth element overlaps c09-17 (Prosper Africa and the USAID, DFC and Commerce toolkit); the focus-country element does not appear there.
